item.title: How inner-city stargazers navigate light pollution to capture night sky
item.description: Astronomy enthusiasts and astrophotographers say despite light pollution, there is plenty to see in inner-city night skies as telescope technology advances. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Emma Johnson

item.title: Previously overlooked protein helps cells divide correctly
item.description: Modern technologies have made it possible to uncover a growing "hidden proteome"—proteins encoded by parts of the genome that researchers previously overlooked. Advances in sequencing and protein analysis are making it possible to find more of these potential proteins and investigate what they do. Researchers at the University of Gothenburg have now identified one such protein. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Great news from Saturn's moon Enceladus in the search for life in space
item.description: What are the chances of finding extraterrestrial life in our solar system? Frank Postberg, a professor of planetary science at Freie Universität Berlin, has published a study in Science Advances with an international team of researchers. They present new evidence that it is easier to determine the constituents of the ocean hidden beneath Enceladus's icy surface than previously assumed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plant root injuries unleash pressure waves that travel long distances
item.description: When plant roots are injured—by insects, for example—the pressure inside the root drops, and a pressure wave spreads rapidly throughout the root system. In neighboring roots, tiny proteins that act as mechanical pressure sensors detect the change and generate electrical and calcium signals. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth microbes survive simulated conditions of Saturn moon’s ocean
item.description: Experiment suggests organisms could live in harsh environment under Enceladus’s icy crust, strengthening possibility moon could support life From the moment scientists spotted plumes of water erupting from Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, it became the most tantalising place in the solar system to search for life beyond Earth. Now the case is even more compelling after researchers found that organisms that live in deep-sea waters off Japan can survive the harsh conditions expected in the briny ocean that lurks beneath Enceladus’s icy crust. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Ian Sample Science editor

item.title: Pompeii's destruction helps calibrate volcanic dating to within decades
item.description: When Pliny the Younger recorded his firsthand experience of the eruption of Mount Vesuvius 2,000 years ago—a cataclysm that buried Pompeii and killed his uncle, Pliny the Elder—he provided enough detail about the date to allow scientists to benchmark methods for dating volcanic eruptions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists supercharge plant immunity to boost its natural defense response
item.description: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) scientists have developed a way to "supercharge" a plant's natural immune response. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Freezing threatens mRNA delivery, but Tris buffer helps nanoparticles retain their potency
item.description: Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have teamed up with pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and Company to uncover how storage conditions affect mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), the technology behind COVID-19 vaccines and other treatments, and how to make them more effective. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 2026-2027 DWU: Middle School Design Challenge
item.description: 2026-2027 DWU: Middle School Design Challenge Overview The 2026-2027 challenge theme is, “Fueling Flight Design Challenge: New Energy Systems.” As more and more aircraft are a part of the US’ National Airspace System (NAS), NASA and partners at the FAA, at universities, and in the aviation industry are searching for ways to increase safety, make […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lillian Gipson

item.title: Testing an antenna layout for the SKA-Low telescope
item.description: SKA-Low is a radio telescope under construction in Western Australia. It will operate across a wide frequency range, from 50 to 350 MHz, and will be the most sensitive telescope of its kind ever built. The completed instrument will link 512 stations spread across an area roughly 75 km (47 miles) wide. Each station's antennas work together like a single large dish, so their arrangement directly shapes what the telescope can detect. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular network resource identifies unknown compounds for biomarker discovery
item.description: Medical researchers, clinicians and pharmaceutical scientists often study small molecules called metabolites, which are produced in living cells through a variety of processes, including the breakdown of food, chemicals or drugs. This area of study is known as metabolomics, and it can be used to identify new signs of disease, measure the effectiveness of medical treatment or study how diet and nutrition affect the body. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 2026-2027 DWU: High School Engineering Challenge
item.description: 2026-2027 DWU: High School Engineering Challenge Challenge Materials Overview The 2026-2027 challenge theme is, “Fueling Flight Design Challenge: New Energy Systems.” As more and more aircraft are a part of the US’ National Airspace System (NAS), NASA and partners at the FAA, at universities, and in the aviation industry are searching for ways to increase safety, […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Lillian Gipson

item.title: Spin rephasing helps quantum memories store single-photon states longer for future networks
item.description: We are continuously sending information to each other, transmitting zeros and ones through a giant network of connected computers and devices. Scientists are now trying to extend this familiar concept of the internet to the quantum realm, looking for an efficient way to exchange quantum rather than classical information: qubits instead of bits. The motivation is not just scientific curiosity. Qubits can be a 0, a 1 or any superposition of the two. They can also become entangled, showing a degree of correlation that is out of reach for classical bits. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Alguien ha estudiado la "recesión sexual" de la Gen Z y se ha encontrado con dos viejos conocidos: crisis de vivienda y empleo
item.description: El concepto no es nuevo, pero sigue rodeado de incógnitas. Desde hace tiempo algunas voces advierten de que la generación Z está sumida en una inexplicable "recesión sexual" , una sequía orgásmica que la aleja de sus padres y abuelos. La pregunta es… ¿Por qué? ¿Nuevas forma de entender la intimidad? ¿Dificultades para encontrar pareja? En EEUU un grupo de investigadores se han propuesto responder esas (y otras) cuestiones en un estudio impulsado por PlayBoy. Para ello charlaron con casi 2.400 jóvenes de entre 18 y 29 años sobre las razones por las (aparentemente) están practicando menos sexo… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Carlos Prego

item.title: Q&A: Were small down payments to blame for the housing bubble?
item.description: The U.S. housing bubble of the early 2000s sent home prices soaring before the market crashed in 2007–08, triggering a foreclosure crisis and a deep recession. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Discovery confirms rare, switchable electrical property in widely used electronics material
item.description: A Husker research team's latest research could open the door to broader use of a class of materials whose electrical properties may someday power next-generation electronics, high-density energy storage, improved computer memory and new strategies for cooling. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rwanda researchers turn plastic waste into durable sisal-reinforced tiles
item.description: Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI World Desk

item.title: Hemos encontrado un fenómeno cósmico que desafía las leyes conocidas de la física estelar. Todo empieza con una estrella muerta
item.description: Aunque tendemos a pensar en el espacio como un lugar inmenso donde reina la paz, en realidad está plagado de procesos violentísimos: explosiones , vientos cargados de partículas iónicas, cuerpos celestes robándose materia los unos a los otros… La mayoría siguen una serie de normas bien conocidas. Sin embargo, de vez en cuando nos encontramos con alguno que nos sorprende . Es justamente lo que acaba de ocurrir con la inesperada onda de choque lanzada desde una estrella muerta situada a 730 años luz de nosotros. El arco que no debería estar allí. Todo empezó en España , en el Telescopio Isaac… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Webb detects ammonia and unexpected chill on a distant giant planet
item.description: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), a team of astronomers led by the University of Maryland identified water, methane and ammonia in the atmosphere of HATS-6 b, a giant planet 500 light-years from Earth. The observations also revealed that HATS-6 b may be significantly cooler than standard calculations predict—suggesting that the planet's relationship with its star may be far more complicated than previously thought. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Students help researchers study how people experience temperature
item.description: Are there any geographical differences in how people experience weather conditions? This question was investigated in the citizen science project Kallt och svettigt (Cold and sweaty) for a year with the help of school pupils throughout Sweden. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Private spacecraft falls back to Earth after failing to rescue aging NASA telescope
item.description: The robotic spacecraft that failed to rescue an aging NASA telescope plunged back to Earth on Friday less than three months after launching on the bold mission. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Personal experience trumps public reputation when people judge others' refusals
item.description: A research team led by Professor Hitoshi Yamamoto of Rissho University experimentally examined how people evaluate others when a person's public reputation conflicts with their own experience with that person. The study was published Sept. 14, 2026, in the journal Evolution and Human Behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Molecular switch-up: Bacteria remodel a peptide to take on new role
item.description: Remodeling may bring to mind construction crews and scaffolding, but the process is far from unique to buildings. Even molecules can be remodeled. Pandorachelins, newly discovered molecules produced by Pandoraea bacteria, are one example. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Uprising: The real medieval revolt that inspired Andrew Garfield's new film
item.description: The Uprising, a medieval drama directed by Paul Greengrass and starring Andrew Garfield, is set to hit theaters this fall. The film draws its inspiration from the Peasants' Revolt of 1381 in England. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Targeted nanoparticles reduce tumor scarring and enable immunotherapy response in mice
item.description: Many liver and lung cancers arise in tissue that's already been scarred by chronic disease, such as hepatitis, cirrhosis or long-term lung damage. That scarring creates an environment that suppresses nearby immune cells, so by the time a tumor takes hold, it's often already shielded from the immune system and immunotherapy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hubble Spots Chaotic Secret in Galaxy
item.description: A chaotic secret hides within this seemingly serene image of spiral galaxy NGC 4698 taken by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope and released on Sept. 18, 2026. As a spiral galaxy like our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disk of stars, gas, and dust. These arms […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Researchers track emerging pathogens at Arctic bird gathering
item.description: Every year, birds migrate north and gather in a single location in the Arctic, and a team of University of Kentucky researchers is collaborating with Alaska Native communities to study how diseases spread and evolve at this gathering before they reach human populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: African elephants and medicinal plants: Possible self-medication documented through local ecological knowledge
item.description: Wild African elephants living in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya appear to seek out specific plants when unwell. Local experts also reported mothers administering plant-based "medicine" to their offspring. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trade tensions, high prices and interest rates drive slip in consumers' outlook
item.description: Consumer sentiment fell by less than four index points in September, reaching its lowest reading in four months and down 15% from January 2026, according to the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two ancient burial sites may explain mystery of Göbeklitepe's scattered human bones
item.description: Since 1995, archaeologists have excavated hundreds of human bones from Göbeklitepe, an archaeological site in southeastern Türkiye. The ancient remains are around 10,000 years old and date to a time when humans were beginning to settle into permanent farming communities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gen Z communicates differently in the workplace, but older colleagues can still decode them
item.description: For all the talk about generational differences at work, some of the biggest differences show up in surprisingly ordinary moments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 3D images reveal how bacterial cells coordinate protein production and transport across the membrane
item.description: Scientists have often thought of cells as small, bustling cities with parts that resemble factories, power grids and shipping systems. While past research has illuminated the individual components of these cell cities, scientists haven't had the tools to probe more deeply into how those elements interact. Fuente: Phys.org.

This Technical Bulletin communicates the risks of […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Meagan Chappell

item.title: Teen loneliness may follow young people into the workplace
item.description: What happens when loneliness follows a young person from the school hallway into the workplace? New research suggests that feeling lonely during adolescence may be linked to a greater risk of unstable or less secure employment in young adulthood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Modification of magnetic nanoparticles improves RNA isolation
item.description: The COVID-19 pandemic clearly demonstrated the importance of rapid and reliable diagnostic methods for detecting and monitoring infectious diseases. Nucleic acids, including RNA, are key biomarkers used in the detection, monitoring and treatment of a wide range of diseases. However, isolating nucleic acids from biological samples can be challenging, particularly when they are present at very low concentrations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate overshoot will leave lasting impacts even after global temperatures fall
item.description: Returning global temperatures to a climate target does not necessarily undo the damage caused by exceeding it, new Concordia-led research published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Age, not feed additives, affects antimicrobial resistance genes in chickens
item.description: For many years, antibiotics have been added to animal feed to help control harmful bacteria and improve growth. But amid concerns about antibiotic resistance—when bacteria adapt to survive treatments that would normally kill them—poultry producers are trying alternatives, including probiotics, which contain helpful bacteria, and essential oils, which come from plants and may have antimicrobial properties. Researchers at Penn State have now found that feeding broiler chickens an antibiotic, a probiotic or essential oils did not significantly affect the overall diversity of antimicrobial… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Satellite data expose an escalating 'boom-and-bust' dynamic in greening drylands
item.description: Dryland ecosystems cover 40% of the Earth's land surface and support more than 2 billion people. According to a new study published in Nature Climate Change, they're becoming increasingly unstable. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What we evaluate, not just what we see, shapes pupil responses
item.description: Our pupils become smaller under brighter conditions and larger under darker conditions. In addition to responding to changes in light, pupil size is influenced by attention, emotion and how visual objects are perceived. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New type of human 'jumping gene' found in a poxvirus
item.description: Scientists at Cornell University have found a human genetic element in a poxvirus and discovered that it is both an important gene for brain function and a jumping gene capable of moving and inserting itself into genomes. A study published in Science reports that the gene, called BC200, combines characteristics never before seen together. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This “rare” autism-linked genetic disorder may be far more common than scientists thought
item.description: A major analysis suggests Phelan-McDermid syndrome, a genetic disorder closely linked to autism, may affect about 1 in 7,300 people and more than 45,000 Americans. Researchers warn that thousands of cases may remain hidden because genetic testing is often not performed, even as targeted treatments move into clinical trials. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: New form of flexible boron is 10 million times more electrically conductive
item.description: The atoms of the 5th element of the periodic table often find themselves in the company of each other, forming allotropes with a rich variety of structural motifs, each carrying a unique set of chemical and physical properties. Despite the long catalog, most boron allotropes do not simultaneously possess high electrical conductivity and plasticity, but a recent study has expanded the portfolio. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: CRISPR could help doctors attack blood cancer without destroying healthy cells
item.description: Researchers used CRISPR to remove CD33 from donor stem cells, potentially giving doctors a way to attack aggressive blood cancers without destroying the healthy cells patients need after a transplant. In a 30-patient trial, the edited cells successfully took hold and appeared to shield blood cells from a CD33-targeted cancer treatment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: CERN has begun disconnecting the Large Hadron Collider
item.description: CERN has started replacing some of the Large Hadron Collider’s most important magnets as part of its High-Luminosity upgrade. The new superconducting magnets will produce fields about 40% stronger, allowing particle beams to be squeezed more tightly before they collide. That should create far more collisions for the ATLAS and CMS experiments to analyze, giving physicists a much larger window into the fundamental workings of the universe. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Rare quantum state reveals particles with quarter-electron charge
item.description: An electron's charge is normally fixed, like a coin you can't break into pieces. But if electrons are cooled close to absolute zero and trapped in a two-dimensional layer under a powerful magnetic field, they organize into a collective state of "quasiparticles" that seem to hold only a fraction of an electron's charge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient virus hunters: How we discovered sheeppox DNA hidden in medieval gospels
item.description: Humans and domesticated animals have lived together for millennia, and this relationship has shaped their destinies in countless ways. Animals offered people food, companionship, traction (pulling plows), clothing and transportation. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal
item.description: Researchers have shown that exotic quantum particles called non-Abelian anyons can perform the full range of operations needed for universal quantum computing. Using 54 qubits on Quantinuum’s H2 processor, they combined braiding and fusion to unlock capabilities that braiding alone could not provide. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: September's ozone hole was the biggest in 20 years
item.description: The area covered by the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at more than 27 million square kilometers (10.4 million square miles) in September, the second-largest area ever observed for this time of year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China overtakes US as top workplace for elite AI researchers, study finds
item.description: For China’s elite artificial intelligence researchers, Silicon Valley no longer holds the unrivalled appeal it once did. A growing number are opting to stay home to build their careers, helping China overtake the United States as the leading workplace for top-tier AI talent, according to a study released this week by the think tank Carnegie China. China employed 41 per cent of the world’s leading AI researchers tracked by the study last year, pulling ahead of the US at 34 per cent, according to... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Chong Ming Lee

item.title: Earth is tearing apart beneath the Pacific Northwest
item.description: Scientists have captured a subduction zone off Vancouver Island in the process of tearing itself apart, revealing that these massive tectonic systems may die piece by piece rather than all at once. The discovery could help explain ancient plate fragments, volcanic activity, and how hidden breaks beneath Cascadia may influence future earthquakes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Nigeria faces world's highest projected heat death toll from super El Niño
item.description: Researchers at the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab combined temperature forecasts with research on how heat affects death rates in more than 24,000 regions worldwide and found that the super El Niño could cause an estimated 451,000 additional heat-related deaths worldwide between now and February 2027. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Three Earth Explorer candidates go forward
item.description: Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Think you know how long you'll wait? Research says think again.
item.description: From coffee shops to customer service call centers, most people believe they have a good sense of how long a service will take. But new research from the University of Florida Warrington College of Business shows that customers often underestimate how much service times can vary, a behavioral bias with important implications for service systems and customers alike. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Random access quantum memory lets one processor select among seven storage cells
item.description: Classical computers can temporarily store the information required to perform specific tasks in a short-term memory component known as RAM (random access memory). This component allows computer processors to retrieve information from a chosen location without searching through all stored data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Today's urban inequality goes far beyond legacy of 'redlining,' study shows
item.description: The use of racially discriminatory housing maps in the 1930s, a practice known as "redlining," perpetuated multigenerational cycles of poverty and segregation that continue today. While redlining shaped cities, its legacy does not fully explain current urban patterns of privilege and disadvantage, a new study finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA sent 12.5M tomato seeds to space in 1984; by 1990, 40,000 schools in 40 countries grew them
item.description: In 1984, NASA initiated the SEEDS project aimed at exploring how the space environment affects plant growth. Participants, comprising approximately 3.3 million students from diverse educational backgrounds worldwide, received kits that included seeds launched into space and Earth-based controls for comparison. Preliminary findings indicated a marginally enhanced germination rate for the seeds sent to space, though notable growth differences diminished during the plants' life cycles. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Curious kids: Does music affect how plants grow?
item.description: "How does the type of music affect plant growth?"—Thomas, 14, Auckland, New Zealand Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds alpine peaks are greening in the Northeast U.S., Canada
item.description: In northeastern North America, a stretch of mountains runs 500 miles (800 kilometers) from the Adirondacks in New York to the Gaspé Peninsula in eastern Quebec. Nearly 70 million people live within a day's drive of one of the alpine zones, the areas above the tree line where trees don't grow because of harsh conditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 400-year-old shipwreck found during pipeline survey in Germany's Bay of Greifswald
item.description: In 2023, in preparation for the construction of an underwater gas pipeline, divers were sent to clear a cluster of anomalies in the Bay of Greifswald, a sheltered lagoon in northern Germany. But as they dove deeper into the murky depths, they discovered things they had not expected: shoe soles, pulley blocks, and a rusty anchor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: California crews uncover possible 45-million-year-old ‘thunder beast’ fossils in Oceanside
item.description: Fossilised bones from a large hoofed mammal were uncovered during an excavation project in Oceanside, California. Paleontologists are studying the remains, which may belong to a thunder beast or a swamp rhino. The discovery took place approximately 12 feet below the surface in the Santiago Formation's sedimentary rock. Researchers are working to determine the exact identity of the fossils found during construction. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: High-tech canopy maps reveal how tropical birds use Amazon forests
item.description: Tropical forests may look like a uniform sea of green from above, but new research shows that carefully measured differences in forest structure and function can help explain how birds use existing habitats, how they respond to threats and which communities may be most at risk as forests change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New tool closes gap in harnessing untapped potential of phages
item.description: A new tool to mutate bacteriophages—viruses that infect bacteria—provides a "big leap" forward in our understanding of how they function and our ability to harness their full potential. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bacteria suspected in deaths of hundreds of baby whales off Argentina
item.description: A bacterial infection is suspected of killing hundreds of baby whales in the southern Argentine region of Patagonia, a marine mammal expert told AFP on Thursday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth from Space: Venetian Lagoon
item.description: Image: This image of the Venetian Lagoon in northern Italy was acquired by the IRIDE satellites on 17 May 2026. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: EE.UU. se lanza a la 'guerra de las galaxias': confirma que tiene armas en el espacio
item.description: La Fuerza Espacial de Estados Unidos, creada por Donald Trump en 2019, no solo tiene unos uniformes con inspiración hollywoodiense , desde 'La guerra de las galaxias' hasta 'Star Trek' o 'Starship Troopers'. Tiene algo mucho más decisivo y que abre un nuevo escenario en la rivalidad bélica con China o Rusia: Washington ha reconocido por primera vez que ha desplegado armas en el espacio.Lo ha anunciado esta semana el secretario de las Fuerzas Aéreas, Troy Meink , durante una conferencia aeroespacial celebrada en Maryland. «Estamos mejorando nuestra preparación frente a las actuales amenazas… Fuente: ABC España - Internacional.
item.dc:creator: Javier Ansorena, Dounia Sbai

item.title: Colorado researchers grow world’s priciest spice on solar panels, doubling yield and earning $60,000
item.description: A study by Colorado State University reveals that saffron flourishes under semi-shaded solar panels, yielding better results than those without shade. By integrating rooftop farming with renewable energy, urban food production can tackle space constraints. Projections suggest considerable net revenue from saffron and electricity production in five years, although challenges related to installation and upkeep remain for successful implementation. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Fossil fuel subsidies are the ‘worst energy policy in the world,’ researchers say
item.description: In an editorial in Science, U.S.-based energy policy experts Paasha Mahdavi and Michael Ross argue that governments creating consumer fossil fuel subsidies in response to rising energy prices is the “worst energy policy in the world.” Mahdavi, an associate professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, in the U.S., and Ross, a professor at […] Fuente: Mongabay.
item.dc:creator: Shreya Dasgupta

item.title: Farmers down 240 million litres of milk after heat
item.description: Milk yield was affected by a series of extreme heatwaves which led to poor grazing conditions, researchers say. Fuente: BBC News - Business.

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Globular Cluster Omega […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Cosmic lockdown: How the environment can isolate quantum fields
item.description: A simplified cosmological model suggests that decoherence can suppress quantum tunneling, effectively locking fields into the vacuum state they have reached. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists gave worms magnetic bacteria. They lived 43% longer
item.description: A magnet-producing bacterium extended the average lifespan of C. elegans worms by more than 43% while helping protect their neurological and intestinal health. Researchers traced much of the effect to suppression of ferroptosis, a damaging form of cell death linked to iron buildup and oxidative stress. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: “We found something never seen before” – A dead star is producing a shock wave that shouldn’t exist
item.description: A dead white dwarf with no detectable disk has somehow produced a powerful shock wave that appears to have persisted for at least 1,000 years. Its magnetic field may be partly responsible, but astronomers say an unexplained “mystery engine” may also be at work. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ancient meteorites reveal a powerful force that helped build the Solar System
item.description: Ancient grains inside one of the oldest known meteorites reveal that a surprisingly strong magnetic field existed during the solar system’s first 200,000 years. The discovery suggests magnetism worked alongside gravity to help transform a vast cloud of gas and dust into the sun and planetary disk. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Tracking the movement of plants
item.description: The flora of the Alps is changing: Species are moving to higher elevations, new plants are appearing and others are disappearing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Age-adjusted suicide rate increased from 2014 to 2017 and then plateaued
item.description: The age-adjusted suicide rate increased from 2014 to 2017 and then did not change significantly from 2017 through 2024, according to a September data brief published by the National Center for Health Statistics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China tested a handheld submarine detector. It tracked a subway train underground
item.description: Chinese researchers have showed a handheld quantum magnetometer built for hunting submarines in a striking real-world test: it tracked a subway train rumbling beneath a city street. The device, developed by Peng Xinhua and colleagues at the University of Science and Technology of China, is described in a study published on September 14 in Acta Physica Sinica. Though it is scarcely larger than a pencil and draws only 5 watts of power, it can isolate the magnetic disturbance caused by a moving... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Zhang Tong

item.title: Elastic fantastic: The deadly fluid of pitcher plants
item.description: In the world of carnivorous plants, Venus flytraps—with their showy, snapping reflexes—have long hogged the limelight. But plants have many creative bug-capture strategies, from slippery waxes to vibrating lids to bizarrely textured fluids. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists discover an “impossible” cellular survival pathway that could help fight cancer
item.description: Scientists discovered a surprising backup system that lets mammalian cells make the essential amino acid cysteine even when the pathways once considered indispensable are disabled. The same survival mechanism may help cancer cells resist treatment, raising the possibility that shutting it down could make tumors easier to kill. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Europe's lab-to-market gap draws proposals from network of more than 120 scientist-innovators
item.description: Europe could turn more of its scientific discoveries into new technologies, products and businesses by changing the way it funds innovation and supports researchers, according to a new Policy Forum published in Science. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: Grasslands in more diverse landscapes can suffer less from drought
item.description: During the heat wave of 2018, meadows and pastures also suffered from drought. Are grasslands in diverse landscapes more resilient to yield losses than those in monotonous regions? Researchers at the University of Bonn, led by Marco Ferro and Dr. Jan Börner from the Institute for Food and Resource Economics (ILR), investigated the influence of landscape diversity on the drought tolerance of grasslands as part of Collaborative Research Center 1502 DETECT. The work is published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biodiversity in production forests: Both costs and benefits shape the financial picture
item.description: Forests provide timber as well as many other ecosystem services. An important question is how measures to conserve biodiversity affect the profitability of forest operations focused on wood production. Researchers from Wageningen University & Research and the University of Freiburg reviewed studies worldwide that compared forest management with biodiversity conservation measures against business-as-usual management without those measures. The work is published in the journal Current Forestry Reports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Patriot parking predictions putting students in the proper spot
item.description: College students are already under stress from classes, tests and presentations. So when something as "easy" as finding a parking spot is anything but, it can cause a bad start to an already challenging day. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US-India satellite captures time-lapse video of volcanic eruption
item.description: Like tendrils on a vine, lava spreads out from the northern crater of Krasheninnikov, a volcano pair on the Pacific coast of Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. On July 30, 2025, an 8.8-magnitude earthquake struck in the nearby ocean, apparently jolting one of the two volcanoes awake. A few days later, for the first time in nearly five centuries, Krasheninnikov started erupting. Since then, the northern volcano has been spilling a steady, eastward-flowing field of molten rock and debris, and the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission has been tracking the changes in the landscape. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Changing counterions gives molecular materials new electronic behaviors
item.description: Orthogonally arranged π-electronic systems that combine electron-donating and electron-accepting units display distinctive electronic and photophysical behavior. Fine-tuning their electronic structure offers a way to control photoinduced electron transfer. Building on this idea, complexing boron with 1,3-diketones and 9-oxidophenalenone may produce electron-deficient cationic π-electronic systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What is not perceived as abuse in youth sports may be part of sexual violence
item.description: Sexual violence against minors in sports is a reality that goes largely unnoticed, despite data suggesting it is not an isolated phenomenon. According to a report by the GIKAFIT research group at EHU in the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country, 20% of participants had experienced behavior of a sexual nature from their coaches, including kissing on the lips, expressions of sexual interest and direct proposals for sexual relations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Materials analysis sheds light on minting mystery of 1834 British sixpence
item.description: A severely deformed 1834 British silver sixpence preserves physical evidence most consistent with an unusual minting anomaly, according to an IA STUDIO study published in npj Heritage Science. The coin was individually marked £8 in a mixed coin album at a flea market in Greater Manchester. The album was later acquired as a bulk lot, rather than the sixpence being purchased separately for £8. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers expand touchpoints to enhance literacy promotion
item.description: Literacy promotion programs, combined with community-based support programs, can affect literacy development in Latino children from birth to 18 months of age, Rutgers researchers have found. Fuente: Phys.org.

The research is published in the journal ACS ES&T Air. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Coolest lava world yet with signs of an atmosphere offers clues to early Earth
item.description: In the search for extraterrestrial life, it makes sense to first look for rocky planets with an atmosphere, like Earth. Without an atmosphere, a planet can't have surface water. But of the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, the vast majority are not rocky, and only a handful of the rocky worlds appear to have an atmosphere. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research examines CIA failures, Saudi links and missed opportunities before September 11 attacks
item.description: A new study from the University of Bath sheds light on critical U.S. intelligence failures ahead of the 9/11 attacks, including evidence that changes how the CIA's repeated failure to share information with the FBI about two hijackers should be understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ningaloo Reef corals reveal early fall spawning window for two key species
item.description: Curtin University scientists have uncovered an important missing piece in the puzzle of how some coral reefs can recover from climate events, providing information that could help guide future conservation and restoration efforts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The medieval world had its own 'deepfakes'—church officials cited a fake imperial decree for centuries
item.description: With deepfakes on the rise, forgery and deception are often viewed as distinctly modern problems—a new era of misinformation made possible by artificial intelligence. One of the first alarming cases occurred at the start of the war in Ukraine, when a doctored video appeared to show President Volodymyr Zelenskyy telling his soldiers to lay down their weapons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More than 60 years of beach survey data reveal the extent of shoreline erosion
item.description: The University of Rhode Island has made one of the world's longest-running beach survey efforts available online through Rhode Island Beach Dynamics Over Decades, a new public website. Fuente: Phys.org.
